brief.head: Beware the monoculture
brief.text: A re­silient fi­nan­cial sys­tem has many ways of doing the same job, Ajay Shah said. India needs twenty big chan­nels for cap­i­tal, not a few nar­row lanes. {119-C05}

brief.head: Contagion, rationally
brief.text: When a cri­sis jumps from one coun­try to the next, Ajay Shah said, that is not a dis­ease but in­vestors up­dat­ing their be­liefs. “Are you a Bayesian up­dater?” {119-C07}[[x2]]

brief.head: Peter, Paul, interest
brief.text: Borrowing from Peter to repay Paul is fine, Ajay Shah said; bor­row­ing to pay in­ter­est is a tread­mill. The test is in­ter­est rate against top-line growth. {119-C10}

brief.head: When it pours
brief.text: From August 1997 to 9/11, Ajay Shah re­called, India took blow after blow: the Asian cri­sis[[x3]], a rate shock, nu­clear tests, the dot-com bust. Each reached the banks. {119-S11}

brief.head: Paved with leverage
brief.text: IL&FS, which de­faulted in 2018, was at heart a lever­aged bet on pri­vate-led Indian in­fra­struc­ture[[x4]], Ajay Shah said. The bet failed, and the cri­sis spread. {119-S12}

lead.kicker: Ajay Shah on financial crises, and Amit Varma’s dissent
lead.head: When bad gets worse, then worse

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 119

body: Every once in a while, Amit Varma said, the world seems to be fall­ing apart: a fi­nan­cial cri­sis, in­fla­tion, bailouts. Ajay Shah, who has spent thirty years in the field as a par­tic­i­pant, set out to ex­plain why.
He began with a def­i­ni­tion. Finance, Shah said, is the brain of the econ­omy: it makes prices, al­lo­cates re­sources and solves people’s fi­nanc­ing prob­lems.

“A fi­nan­cial cri­sis is when there is a sud­den and non­lin­ear im­pair­ment of the func­tions of fi­nance,” he said. One firm fail­ing is not a cri­sis, nor even a whole in­dus­try, if the work can be done an­other way. {119-C01}

The stakes are enor­mous, Shah ar­gued. Financial crises are “up­stream of wars and rev­o­lu­tions”, and he drew a di­rect line from the Great Depression[[x1]] to Adolf Hitler and the Second World War.
Nobody is a by­stander. “You may not be in­ter­ested in fi­nance, but the fi­nan­cial sys­tem is in­ter­ested in you,” he said. {119-C02}
## Stories first

All eco­nom­ics is rooted in eco­nomic his­tory, Shah said, so he started with sto­ries: New York in 1929, India in 1991, Harshad Mehta, the East Asian cri­sis, UTI in 2000, 2008 and the IL&FS de­fault of 2018.

In each he hunted for the am­pli­fier. A crash on one ex­change is too small to shake the world, he said; it takes feed­back loops, where “if things are bad, they get worse, and be­cause they’re worse, they get worse.” {119-C03}
He was can­did about his own record. Raj Chitale had warned him that UTI’s US-64 scheme would blow up, and he had not un­der­stood how bro­ken it was. “I’m point­ing a fin­ger at me,” he said.
The re­sponse to 2008, run by Ben Bernanke and oth­ers schooled in the lessons of 1929, he held up as a model: let firms fail, but pro­tect the func­tions of fi­nance, what­ever it takes.
## Why it keeps hap­pen­ing

From his­tory Shah built a tax­on­omy of five types: bank­ing, cur­rency, debt, se­cu­ri­ties mar­ket and mixed crises. Each runs to a script. “I see fi­nan­cial cri­sis the way a doc­tor sees a can­cer,” he said.

Crises will never end, he ar­gued, for four rea­sons: human cog­ni­tion, human clev­er­ness, state fail­ure and the fal­lacy of com­po­si­tion. Regulators will al­ways be out­wit­ted by the clever­est peo­ple in fi­nance. {119-C12}

So the state should pre­pare rather than pre­tend. Shah’s tool­kit runs from sound reg­u­la­tion of each firm to a lender of last re­sort, a law for re­solv­ing failed firms and a stand­ing army of ex­perts.
He re­jected three ex­tremes: pure lais­sez-faire, the pop­ulist story that bailouts pro­tect fat cats, and the Indian re­flex to “ban it”.
## The dis­sent
Varma had promised to keep his dis­agree­ments for the end, and he did. He has “great sym­pa­thy for the Austrian view”: that crises are caused by easy money, and made worse by the state.
“When I think about 2008, to me it was a fail­ure of the state,” he said. {119-C16}
The ar­gu­ment that bailouts later made money did not move him: the cost, he said, falls on everyone’s taxes, the poor­est in­cluded. Suppressing small fail­ures, he warned, stores up big­ger ones.

Both men ended on com­mon ground. Ordinary cit­i­zens have skin in the game, Varma said, and should learn the ba­sics. Shah agreed: no­body should treat fi­nan­cial cri­sis as “some ex­otic, far away sub­ject”.

second.label: Learning from 1929
second.head: Sorry, Milton, we did it
second.deck: Ben Bernanke’s apology to Milton Friedman, and how it shaped 2008

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the Fed’s apology to Friedman

body: In a 2002 speech, Ben Bernanke, then on the Federal Reserve’s board of gov­er­nors but not yet its chair­man, turned to Milton Friedman, who was on the stage with him. About the Great Depression, Bernanke said, the Fed had done it. {119-S07}
Ajay Shah called the mo­ment dou­bly lovely. Bernanke gave Friedman the credit, but the two of them, with Anna Schwartz, had built the body of knowl­edge on what went wrong in 1929.

Six years later Bernanke chaired the Fed through the 2008 cri­sis and let its bal­ance sheet grow roughly five-fold. {119-S08} “This is how great coun­tries are made,” Shah said. Amit Varma called it a rare case of a thinker be­com­ing a doer.

quote.text: Regarding the Great Depression, you’re right. We did it. We’re very sorry. But thanks to you, we won’t do it again.

third.head: Fat cats, thin losses

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the bailout ledger

body: The pop­ulist story of 2008, Ajay Shah said, is that tax­pay­ers paid for the fat cats’ Lamborghinis. The data, he ar­gued, say oth­er­wise.

In the US, the Treasury put about $0.45 tril­lion into TARP, headed by Neel Kashkari. After the as­sets were sold, a GAO re­port put the loss at $31 bil­lion, while the Fed’s cri­sis pur­chases were wildly prof­itable. {#tarp31} Taken to­gether, the in­ter­ven­tion made money.

He made the same point about UTI, with a con­fes­sion. He had ar­gued over its res­cue with M. Damodaran, then head­ing UTI. The shares the gov­ern­ment took were sold five years later at a big profit. “Damodaran was right, I was wrong.” {119-S10}
Amit Varma was un­moved. Who pays mat­ters, he said, what­ever the to­tals: bailouts are funded by everyone’s taxes, in­clud­ing those of the poor­est. {119-C17}

box.title: What 1929 taught the Fed
box.text: Milton Friedman, Anna Schwartz and a young Ben Bernanke worked out what went wrong in 1929[[x6]]. Ajay Shah’s sum­mary of their lessons: act as lender of last re­sort, never let money con­tract, and pro­tect the func­tions of fi­nance. {119-C09}

sections.label: The definition
sections.head: The brain of the economy
sections.caption: what a financial crisis is
body: Finance, Ajay Shah said, is the brain of the econ­omy. It de­cides who gets money, which in­dus­tries and which tech­nolo­gies; it makes the prices that tell en­trepreneurs where to in­vest; and it solves people’s prob­lems of mov­ing money across time, man­ag­ing risk and fund­ing large, com­plex projects.
A fi­nan­cial cri­sis, by his def­i­ni­tion, is a sud­den and non­lin­ear im­pair­ment of those func­tions. {119-C01}

The def­i­ni­tion does a lot of work. One firm fail­ing is not a cri­sis. Even a whole in­dus­try can col­lapse with­out one, if the econ­omy can route the work through other chan­nels. The point, Shah said, is to get things done. “We have no loy­alty to fi­nance as a means. We have a loy­alty to the ends.”
## The at­ten­tion span

We no­tice civil avi­a­tion, Shah said, only when an Air India plane crashes into a med­i­cal col­lege hos­tel in Amdavad. Financial crises get the same short at­ten­tion, though the world has been shaped by them. {119-J12}
Yet as in­di­vid­u­als, he said, we all have skin in the game: when the fi­nan­cial sys­tem glitches, it im­poses costs on firms and peo­ple all over the land­scape. {119-C02}
~ Amit Varma, who calls him­self a gen­tle lis­tener in these con­ver­sa­tions, promised to save his dis­agree­ments for a final chap­ter. He kept the prom­ise.

quote.text: A fi­nan­cial cri­sis is when there is a sud­den and non­lin­ear im­pair­ment of the func­tions of fi­nance.

art.caption: Ajay Shah on what a financial crisis is

sections.label: The playbook
sections.head: Lend freely, and make them cry
sections.caption: the Friedman-Bernanke playbook
body: Is there a case for the state? First ask whether there is a mar­ket fail­ure, Ajay Shah said, and here there is: a neg­a­tive ex­ter­nal­ity. A small firm like Swapnalok Studios, head­ing for an IPO, can be hurt by a cri­sis for no fault of its own. Amit Varma cau­tioned that the state need not act on every ex­ter­nal­ity.
Shah then set out the read­ing of the Great Depression built by Milton Friedman, Anna Schwartz and a young Ben Bernanke. The Fed, in their view, made three mis­takes.

First, it failed as lender of last re­sort. Walter Bagehot’s rule, in Shah’s words, is to lend freely against good col­lat­eral at a penal rate: “So peo­ple should cry when they come ask­ing for credit from a cen­tral bank.” {119-J13}
Second, it let the money sup­ply con­tract[[x7]], and the de­fla­tion that fol­lowed raised the real bur­den of every debt. Third, as banks died, what they knew about their bor­row­ers died too.
## Functions, not firms
The rem­edy is to let firms fail but pro­tect the func­tions. “We have no loy­alty to banks, we have no loy­alty to NBFCs,” Shah said. {119-C09}
~ In 2008 the Fed did just that. It let Bear Stearns and Lehman go, grew its bal­ance sheet from about $0.9 tril­lion to $4.5 tril­lion, and kept in­fla­tion under con­trol. {119-S08}

quote.text: It takes a thinker to say we will do what it takes. And if it takes five X, we’ll do five X.

sections.label: The five types
sections.head: Every crisis has a script
sections.caption: the five types of crisis
body: Around the world, Ajay Shah said, there are about five fi­nan­cial crises a year in one coun­try or an­other. {#fiveayear} He sorts them into five types.

Banking crises come first. Shah bor­rowed Merton Miller’s de­scrip­tion of bank­ing[[x8]] as a dis­as­ter-prone nine­teenth-century in­dus­try. Indian banks run about 20 times lever­age, so a five per cent loss wipes them out, and their loans are opaque and illiq­uid. {119-C08}
Banks also at­tract po­lit­i­cal loot­ing, for the rea­son the bank rob­ber gave: “be­cause that’s where the money is.” {119-J10}

Currency crises are macro­eco­nomics. Debt crises turn on whether the in­ter­est rate out­runs the growth of the top line. India masks the prob­lem by forc­ing the fi­nan­cial sys­tem to lend cheaply to the gov­ern­ment. “We ba­si­cally vi­o­late the Magna Carta,” Shah said. {119-J17}
## The inner sanc­tum

Securities mar­kets, he said, are “the com­mand­ing heights of the fi­nan­cial sys­tem”. In an illiq­uid mar­ket like India’s cor­po­rate bonds, one large sale can set off fall­ing prices, fall­ing NAVs and more re­demp­tions. {119-C11}
The cure is a deep, liq­uid mar­ket open to ev­ery­one: “there should be al­go­rith­mic traders, there should be as­trol­ogy traders.”
~ The fifth type mixes the oth­ers, as in Indonesia. Anyone who has not lived through a cri­sis, Shah said, should learn the scripts from books.

quote.text: Banks are a dis­as­ter prone 19th cen­tury in­dus­try. And they will go wrong be­cause you have too much lever­age.

sections.label: The causes
sections.head: Spy versus spy, forever
sections.caption: why crises keep happening
body: Ajay Shah of­fered no grand uni­fied the­ory of why crises hap­pen, but four el­e­ments of one.

The first is human cog­ni­tion. Someone who spends twenty good years in a boom for­gets that things can go wrong, and the trader with the big­gest lever­age looks like a hero. Statisticians who fit mod­els on the last five or ten good years make the same error.
“Those who fail to learn from his­tory are doomed to par­tic­i­pate in its rep­e­ti­tion,” he said. {119-J11}
## Cat and mouse
The sec­ond is clev­er­ness. Regulators and bankers play a cat-and-mouse game, Shah said, like *Spy versus Spy* in *Mad Magazine*. {119-J09} “Are you thir­teen again?” Amit Varma asked.
Bankers with lop­sided pay­offs find the chinks in every rule, and some of the smartest peo­ple in the world work in fi­nance. Regulation will al­ways play catch-up. {119-C12}

The third is state fail­ure: pub­lic choice prob­lems and reg­u­la­tors with too much power. The fourth is the fal­lacy of com­po­si­tion: mak­ing each bank safe does not make the sys­tem safe, be­cause many moves in one di­rec­tion add up to an avalanche.
~ To be­lieve that bril­liant reg­u­la­tors could end crises, Shah said, is an il­lu­sion of con­trol. Whatever we build will foul up, over and over.

quote.text: The brain power of Goldman Sachs will al­ways ex­ceed the brain power of the reg­u­la­tors.

sections.label: The remedies
sections.head: A standing army for bad days
sections.caption: the crisis toolkit
body: What can be done? Ajay Shah’s first step is mi­cro­pru­den­tial reg­u­la­tion: get­ting each firm right, one at a time. It is not enough, he said, but it is nec­es­sary, and India has a long his­tory of fail­ing at it.
Second, a lender of last re­sort. “We in India have not begun,” he said.

Third, a res­o­lu­tion frame­work, so that fi­nan­cial firms can go bank­rupt while small savers, the grand­moth­ers and den­tists, are pro­tected. The Financial Resolution Bill that came out of FSLRC[[x9]] ran into op­po­si­tion from bank unions and stalled.
## The nin­jas

Fourth, and messi­est, a stand­ing army: ex­perts, data and au­thor­ity, per­haps in the Department of Economic Affairs, for the crises no­body de­signed for. Shah pointed to the Office of Financial Research that America built after 2008. {119-C13}
He ended with a heresy. A good bank­ing sys­tem is “a first world thing”, he said, and India is at best 25 years from one; until then, banks should stay small. {119-C14}
~ “I hate to pick win­ners, I hate to pick losers. But I am propos­ing a loser,” Shah said. Amit Varma was wary: “Don’t use state co­er­cion to get there.” {119-J07}

quote.text: And so we need an un­pre­dictable team of nin­jas which will be able to deal with these things as they come along.

art.caption: Ajay Shah on the crisis toolkit

sections.label: The dissent
sections.head: Let the small fires burn
sections.caption: the Austrian view
body: Amit Varma saved his dis­agree­ment for the last chap­ter. He has great sym­pa­thy, he said, for the Austrian view: that crises begin with easy money from cen­tral banks and are deep­ened by the state.

The roar­ing twen­ties ran on easy credit from the Fed, he said, and the years be­fore 2008 on Alan Greenspan’s cheap money. After 1929, he said, cit­ing Thomas Sowell[[x11]], the econ­omy began re­cov­er­ing within months, until gov­ern­ment in­ter­ven­tion made it worse. {119-R16}
He dis­puted Ajay Shah’s view that Hitler’s spend­ing re­vived Germany[[x10]]: the German econ­omy, Varma said, was com­ing back to speed by 1923, be­fore Hitler came to power. {#germany}
On 2008 he cited the Community Reinvestment Act, Fannie and Freddie and the rat­ing agen­cies. It was a fail­ure of the state, he said, not of cap­i­tal­ism. {119-C16}
## Let it flood

Bailouts cre­ate moral haz­ard, pri­vatis­ing prof­its and so­cial­is­ing losses. That they made money years later, Varma ar­gued, does not wash: the cost falls on everyone’s taxes, the poor­est in­cluded.

From James C. Scott’s *In Praise of Floods* he drew a para­ble. Embankments raise a river above the land until the flood is far worse; putting out every small for­est fire builds fuel for one the size of a state. {119-C18}
~ Be scep­ti­cal of con­ven­tion, he con­cluded, not dis­mis­sive of it, and keep read­ing eco­nomic his­tory. {119-C19}

quote.text: The taxes of the beg­gar at the traf­fic sig­nal who pays a GST when she buys salt and soap.

quote.text: The mar­ket econ­omy is not a tidy, cen­trally planned com­pany town. The mar­ket econ­omy is an un­pre­dictable bub­bling of the human heart, fig­ur­ing out new things all the time.

p3.title: Crash course
p3.deck: Four stories from the history of crises, and what each teaches

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the crash that brought down the whole world
stories.head: New York falls, the world follows
body: Ajay Shah did not claim that fi­nan­cial crises began in 1929: there had been tulip mania, paper money gone bad and bank­ing crises long be­fore. But 1929, he said, is a lovely place to start.

Through the roar­ing twen­ties, as they are called, the American and global econ­omy al­ready had dif­fi­cul­ties, and the Fed, the world’s most im­por­tant cen­tral bank, had not been doing a great job.
Then, for rea­sons still not deeply un­der­stood today, the New York Stock Exchange crashed[[x12]] in 1929. {119-S01}

A fall in share prices on one ex­change is not big enough to shake the world, Shah said. What did it was a chain: the crash trig­gered some­thing, which trig­gered some­thing else. Bank fail­ures made the econ­omy worse, and a worse econ­omy felled more banks. {119-C03}
At the peak, some­thing like 30 per cent of the American bank­ing sys­tem went bank­rupt. {#thirty} Within months, the crash was show­ing up in India. {#india1929}
The gravest con­se­quence was in Germany. “There is a di­rect line be­tween the Great Depression and Adolf Hitler,” Shah said. That, he ar­gued, is why the fate of the world is on the line.

~ There was a twist in the re­cov­ery. Franklin Delano Roosevelt and Hitler, Shah said, ran poli­cies that would now be called Keynesian with­out Keynes’s ideas. They im­pro­vised, “through seat of the pants”. Keynes’s ideas, he added, have had a mid­dling record when ap­plied to later de­pres­sions.
stories.why: A crash in one mar­ket can­not shake the world on its own; it needs am­pli­fiers. To un­der­stand any cri­sis, Shah said, look for the feed­back loop that makes bad worse. {119-C03}
stories.postscript: Amit Varma later dis­puted that Hitler’s spend­ing re­vived Germany: its econ­omy, he said, was com­ing back to speed by 1923, be­fore Hitler took power. {#germany}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the crash of 1929

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on India’s balance of payments crisis of 1991
stories.head: A run through narrow lanes
body: A coun­try im­ports the gap be­tween what it in­vests and what it saves, Ajay Shah said. {119-C04} Through the late 1980s, India’s fis­cal deficits grew, worst of all in the po­lit­i­cal in­sta­bil­ity after Rajiv Gandhi, eat­ing into sav­ings and rais­ing the need for for­eign cap­i­tal.
Then Saddam Hussein in­vaded Kuwait, and re­mit­tances took a hit. Capital con­trols meant money could enter[[x13]] only through a few *patli gallis*, nar­row lanes, and these choked. {119-S02}

Once ev­ery­one was sure the rupee would crash, ev­ery­one bet on it. Exporters kept their dol­lars abroad, im­porters bought dol­lars early, and Indians moved as­sets out, wait­ing to bring the money back after the fall.
~ The les­son, for Shah, is re­silience: India needs twenty big chan­nels for cap­i­tal, with no in­volve­ment of the gov­ern­ment. {119-C05}

quote.text: Once ev­ery­body be­lieves that the rupee has to de­pre­ci­ate greatly, then every think­ing per­son is try­ing to bet on that

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the rupee crisis of 1991

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on George Soros and the Bank of England
stories.head: The day the pound broke
body: George Soros[[x14]], Ajay Shah said, is the great­est hero of the cur­rency cri­sis. He thought deeply about the dilemma fac­ing the Bank of England.

Keeping the pound in the European ex­change rate mech­a­nism would need a sharp rise in in­ter­est rates. The econ­omy was al­ready weak and elec­tions were near. Why, Soros reck­oned, would a gov­ern­ment kick its own econ­omy in the face?
So he bet the pound would break out, and in one day made a profit of over a bil­lion dol­lars. {#billion}

~ Once a few traders bet against a cur­rency, hun­dreds more join, be­cause their bets can make the col­lapse hap­pen; Amit Varma noted that Soros called this re­flex­iv­ity. “No gov­ern­ment can stand up to the com­bined power of the global fi­nan­cial sys­tem,” Shah said. {119-S05}
stories.why: A cur­rency cri­sis is macro­eco­nomics, Shah said. Whoever un­der­stands the trade-off a gov­ern­ment faces be­tween its peg and its econ­omy can tell whether the peg will hold, and mar­kets pun­ish the pol­icy that can­not. {119-C07}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on George Soros and the pound

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah retells Ben Bernanke’s insight on lost knowledge
stories.head: What the bank manager knew
body: Picture a bank in pre-digital America, Ajay Shah said. No com­put­ers, no mod­els, just branches, loan of­fi­cers and paper files. The man­ager lives among his bor­row­ers[[x15]] and knows whether they are up­stand­ing mem­bers of the com­mu­nity.
Shah cast him­self as the bor­rower, a man so tem­per­ate that “I only have milk in a bar.” The man­ager knows that, and knows his re­pay­ment his­tory. {119-J02}

Then the bank fails, for no fault of ei­ther, be­cause it lent against shares in New York. Shah goes to the next bank, run by Vaishnav, who has no his­tory with him: “Let’s get started with a 10 rupee loan.” {119-S09}
~ Multiply that across 30 per cent of America’s banks, he said, and cof­fee shops and small man­u­fac­tur­ers ev­ery­where are choked of work­ing cap­i­tal just when they need it.

quote.text: This his­tory is in your skull. And this his­tory is in your files.

quiz.a: Lend freely against good col­lat­eral at a penal rate, so bor­row­ers cry.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 119. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: George Soros (Aris Oikonomou - European Commission, CC BY 4.0); Milton Friedman (Bachrach Studios, public domain); Walter Bagehot (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); James C. Scott (SOAS University of London, CC BY 3.0); Thomas Sowell (Internet Archive Book Images, public domain); Henry Hazlitt (work-for-hire, CC BY 3.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon and Apple.

shelf.title: The Beauty of Finance (Ep 21 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s mas­ter­class on why fi­nance ex­ists and why it mat­ters to the real econ­omy: fi­nance as ‘the brain of the economy’, not a casino for the rich, traced back to me­dieval trad­ing voy­ages.

shelf.title: The Journey of Indian Finance (Ep 71 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: An insider’s ac­count of how Indian fi­nance was built: 25 years in which the fi­nance min­istry, SEBI, NSE and aca­demics worked to­gether, and how re­form pe­tered out once that group scat­tered.

shelf.title: The journey of Indian finance (paper)
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s eco­nomic his­tory of Indian fi­nance from 1947 to today, which Amit calls close to mag­is­te­rial and the de­fin­i­tive work on the sub­ject.

shelf.title: Ajay Shah Brings the Dreams of the 20th Century (Ep 402 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A ten-and-a-half-hour con­ver­sa­tion with Ajay about his life and ideas, in­clud­ing the in­side story of how India built a good eq­uity mar­ket through SEBI, NSE and NSDL.

shelf.title: The Life and Times of KP Krishnan (Ep 355 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and KP Krishnan
shelf.why: An eight-hour oral his­tory from a re­former in­side the Indian state: how India han­dled the 2008 cri­sis, fought for in­fla­tion tar­get­ing and built the bank­ruptcy code.

shelf.title: Don’t Mess With the Exchange Rate (Ep 67 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why the ex­change rate is the most im­por­tant price in the econ­omy and should be set by the mar­ket: rig­ging it to make ex­porters look com­pet­i­tive is a trans­fer from the poor, and man­ag­ing it in­vites cur­rency crises.

shelf.title: What Our Genes and Phones Tell Us (Ep 117 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Part of the show’s se­ries on mea­sure­ment: how new data, such as borrowers’ phone top-up habits, is re­plac­ing the bank manager’s per­sonal judge­ment.

shelf.title: Who lends to the Indian state?
shelf.creator: Aneesha Chitgupi, Ajay Shah, Manish K Singh, Susan Thomas & Harsh Vardhan
shelf.why: XKDR Forum’s paper, the first to mea­sure India’s fi­nan­cial re­pres­sion: 95% of the Indian state’s bor­row­ing is co­erced out of the fi­nan­cial sys­tem, which makes its debt look cheaper than it re­ally is.

shelf.title: SVB, Banking and the State of the Economy (Ep 323 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma, Ajay Shah and Mohit Satyanand
shelf.why: Ajay and Mohit Satyanand on the SVB col­lapse and bank­ing fun­da­men­tals, in­clud­ing the coun­ter­in­tu­itive case that bank fail­ures are part of a healthy sys­tem, and how elec­tronic pay­ments let a bank’s money flee over a week­end.

shelf.title: Impossible Germany
shelf.creator: Wilco
shelf.why: Amit calls it ‘ab­so­lutely magnificent’, adding: ‘Nothing to do with fi­nance, and thank God for that.’

shelf.title: Mutual funds with feet of clay
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Lays out a feed­back loop: large cor­po­rate bond fund re­demp­tions hit an illiq­uid bond mar­ket, prices and NAVs fall, and that trig­gers more re­demp­tions.

shelf.title: Metrics for Intervention (Ep 101 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Four met­rics (dis­cre­tion, num­ber of trans­ac­tions, stakes and trans­parency) for judg­ing how hard a job is for the state, which ex­plain why bu­reau­cra­cies strug­gle to see the world ac­cu­rately and why fi­nance is among the hard­est areas to reg­u­late well.

shelf.title: Where Indian Regulation Went Wrong (Ep 99 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s di­ag­no­sis of India’s statu­tory reg­u­la­tors as a new cen­tral plan­ning sys­tem that has to be fixed up­stream, at the level of or­gan­i­sa­tional de­sign, and of why fi­nan­cial reg­u­la­tors will never work per­fectly.

shelf.title: Going Bankrupt in India (Ep 80 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why bank­ruptcy is a healthy, nor­mal part of eco­nomic life, and how the pol­i­tics of India’s bank­ruptcy re­form gave big com­pa­nies out­sized in­flu­ence, left op­er­a­tional cred­i­tors weak and squeezed small manufacturers’ work­ing cap­i­tal.

shelf.title: The GPT 5 Deep Research Info Dump on Financial Crises
shelf.creator: ChatGPT
shelf.why: He thought it ‘pretty good’ for his­tor­i­cal back­ground and for sum­maris­ing how Austrians, Keynesians and mon­e­tarists, as well as Minsky and Bernanke in­di­vid­u­ally, read each cri­sis.

shelf.title: Economic Facts and Fallacies
shelf.creator: Thomas Sowell
shelf.why: Sowell names foun­da­tional eco­nomic fal­la­cies from which many other er­rors grow; Amit says he fin­ished it a much clearer thinker about eco­nom­ics.

shelf.title: The Forgotten Man: A New History of the Great Depression
shelf.creator: Amity Shlaes
shelf.why: A con­trary his­tory of the Great Depression that Amit has a lot of sym­pa­thy for: gov­ern­ment in­ter­ven­tions, not the stock-market crash, turned a down­turn into a de­pres­sion.

shelf.title: The Globalisation Episode (Ep 95 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ foun­da­tional think­ing on glob­al­i­sa­tion: first prin­ci­ples, a pot­ted in­tel­lec­tual his­tory up to the Second World War, and why tar­iffs harm a country’s own peo­ple and shift wealth from the poor to the rich.

shelf.title: Economics in One Lesson
shelf.creator: Henry Hazlitt
shelf.why: Hazlitt’s 1946 ‘col­lec­tion of light bulbs’ that uses the ba­sics of scarcity and in­cen­tives to clear up fal­la­cies about price con­trols, tar­iffs, in­fla­tion and gov­ern­ment spend­ing, teach­ing you to ask what the money would have done if left with con­sumers.

shelf.title: Economics in One Lesson (Ep 109 of Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ episode on Hazlitt’s seen-versus-unseen lens, ap­plied to tar­iffs and gov­ern­ment spend­ing: you have to count what would have hap­pened with­out the in­ter­ven­tion.

shelf.title: What Really Happened?
shelf.creator: Lawrence H White
shelf.why: Larry White’s essay on how easy money, bad gov­ern­ment in­cen­tives and quasi-government en­ti­ties caused the 2008 cri­sis, usu­ally called a mar­ket fail­ure.

shelf.title: Not What They Had in Mind
shelf.creator: Arnold Kling
shelf.why: Arnold Kling’s book-length case that the 2008 cri­sis was a fail­ure of the state, driven by over­reach rather than free mar­kets.

shelf.title: The Seen and the Unseen episode with Suyash Rai on Demonetisation
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Suyash Rai
shelf.why: An early episode with Suyash Rai, the source of his point that cost-benefit anal­y­sis hides an im­moral­ity when the costs fall on one group and the ben­e­fits on an­other.

shelf.title: In Praise of Floods
shelf.creator: James C Scott
shelf.why: James C Scott on the di­ver­sity that ex­isted be­fore the agri­cul­tural age, and on how sup­press­ing every small dis­as­ter builds up a much big­ger one, which Amit ap­plies to bailouts and moral haz­ard.

shelf.title: The Clash of Economic Ideas
shelf.creator: Lawrence H White
shelf.why: Lawrence White’s his­tory of the big eco­nomic de­bates of the last cen­tury, from Keynes and Friedman to Fabian so­cial­ism and cen­tral plan­ning, show­ing that each school was right in some ways and wrong in oth­ers.

laughs.text: Amit says he is re­ally a ‘gen­tle listener’ learn­ing from Ajay, then adds: ‘If you don’t agree, why are you a reg­u­lar viewer? It’s be­cause of me, isn’t it? I’m so hot.’

Explaining what a neigh­bour­hood bank man­ager knows about a reg­u­lar bor­rower, Ajay de­scribes him­self: ‘when I get drunk in the evening, I’m ex­tremely tem­per­ate in my ways. I only have milk in a bar. Okay, I’m that kind of guy.’

Ajay on who makes a deep, liq­uid mar­ket: ‘There should be for­eign­ers, there should be Indians, there should be Bengalis, there should be Tamilians, there should be al­go­rith­mic traders, there should be as­trol­ogy traders.’

Ajay on com­pla­cent prac­ti­tion­ers who think ex­e­cu­tion is all that mat­ters and that ‘watch­ing these ver­bose males on long-winded shows is com­pletely a waste of time’. Earlier he lists among humanity’s fail­ings: ‘People fail to watch an EIE episode on fi­nan­cial cri­sis.’
Ajay on the ‘lefties’ who say evil cap­i­tal­ists prof­ited from Thailand’s col­lapse: ‘No, it’s called cap­i­tal­ism. This is how it works.’

Ajay, de­fend­ing his small-banking dream: ‘So I said I hate to pick win­ners, I hate to pick losers. But I am propos­ing a loser.’ Amit: ‘I mean you’re free to imag­ine your dream world, but don’t use state co­er­cion to get there.’

After Ajay re­jects the ‘fat cat’ story, Amit starts a pun: ‘So Ajay, what do you call the con­fes­sion of a cat?’ Ajay de­flects: ‘The word­smithing that is re­quired is what do you call the con­fes­sion of a fat cat, and we need to find a cor­rect an­swer. I want to tell you about fi­nan­cial cri­sis.’ Amit: ‘No fool­ing around. Continue.’

Spy vs Spy: ‘you have to be my age to know some­thing called Mad Magazine and a car­toon strip called Spy ver­sus Spy,’ says Ajay, to de­scribe the cat-and-mouse game be­tween reg­u­la­tors and bankers. Amit: ‘Are you thir­teen again? Spy ver­sus spy was amaz­ing.’
The bank robber’s line, ‘Why do you rob banks? Answer, be­cause that’s where the money is.’ Ajay uses it to ex­plain why every po­lit­i­cal econ­omy tries to grab bank money.
Ajay’s twist on the old adage: ‘Those who fail to learn from his­tory are doomed to par­tic­i­pate in its rep­e­ti­tion.’

Ajay opens by not­ing that we pay at­ten­tion to avi­a­tion safety only when ‘an Air India plane crashes into a med­i­cal col­lege hos­tel in Amdavad’. Financial crises get the same lim­ited at­ten­tion span.
Walter Bagehot’s lender-of-last-resort rule, in Ajay’s words: ‘Lend freely against good col­lat­eral at a penal rate. So peo­ple should cry when they come ask­ing for credit from a cen­tral bank.’

Ajay treats the flawed pre-2008 se­cu­ri­ti­sa­tion mod­els as a sci­en­tific gap, not a moral fail­ure: ‘You needed to fig­ure out the pho­to­elec­tric ef­fect in order to play cor­rectly around it.’ He cred­its ‘our friend’ Viral Acharya with im­prov­ing un­der­stand­ing of those prod­ucts.

New Zealand, 1987: Ajay says only then did cen­tral bank­ing ‘get to the basics’ with in­fla­tion tar­get­ing. ‘Conventional money took a thou­sand years be­fore we got to in­fla­tion targeting’, which is why he is pa­tient but scep­ti­cal about crypto.
Magna Carta: de­scrib­ing India’s fi­nan­cial re­pres­sion, Ajay says ‘We ba­si­cally vi­o­late the Magna Carta,’ be­cause the state forcibly takes money from the econ­omy to fund its debt.
